title: The Digital Detective Club: Teaching AI Literacy to Young Students
author: Nick Potkalitsky, Ph.D.
source: Educating AI (Nick Potkalitsky on Substack), December 1, 2025
summary: AI literacy curricula address the wrong age. By high school, students have absorbed years of AI text without detective skills, and blind trust is ingrained. Potkalitsky pushes literacy down to K through 5, not as LLM mechanics but as practical discernment: verifying facts, recognizing human versus AI text, valuing specificity and authentic voice, building sourcing skepticism. The Text Detective Academy gives young students playful vocabulary (sniff out robot writing, the flavor test, two-question system) and an investigator identity rather than a list. Core contrast exercises juxtapose specific human samples (grandmother's kitchen with cracked tile from a pickle jar a child dropped in second grade) against generic AI samples (warm, welcoming space with family photographs lining the walls) and ask why one feels real. Fact-checking demands sources for every claim and introduces true/false/cannot verify. Two case files (water-cycle homework, Charlotte's Web report) deploy both skills. For K-2 versus 3-5, differentiation and assessment notes provided. Curriculum is explicitly provisional, inviting adaptation rather than scripted delivery.
points: By the time students reach high school, they have already spent years passively consuming AI text without tools to evaluate it, making K-5 the critical window.
Young students can sense the difference between authentic human voice and generic AI text (one student called it the flavor test) but need explicit language to articulate and act on that sense.
Specificity and authentic detail (a cracked tile from a pickle jar dropped in second grade) signal human writing; generic confidence signals AI.

The two-question system (Can I check this fact, and has it been published by a reliable source?) and three-way verdict (true/false/cannot verify) teach elementary students the actual tools adults use.
quotes: We're living through a profound shift in how text gets created. For the first time in history, our children will grow up in a world where much of what they read (homework help, explanations, stories, even personal messages) might be generated by AI rather than written by humans.

Most AI literacy curricula focus on older students: high schoolers learning about algorithmic bias, college students studying machine learning ethics. These are important, but they miss a critical window. By the time students reach high school, they've already spent years passively consuming AI-generated content without tools to evaluate it.

This curriculum is not about explaining how AI works under the hood (that can come later). Instead, it teaches elementary students (kindergarten through fifth grade) practical detective skills for the world they're actually living in.
This is not about demonizing AI. It's about building discernment. Children who complete this curriculum will not fear AI-generated text, but they will not blindly trust it either.

Students who cannot distinguish between human and AI writing will struggle to develop their own authentic voices. Students who cannot verify facts will be vulnerable to plausible-sounding misinformation. Students who never learn to demand sources will accept authority without question.

A student detective named Artyom discovered something important. He said: The robot makes English that is correct but not real. It's like textbook English. It follows all the rules perfectly, but it does not have the flavor of how people actually write.
Robot writing sounds nice but feels empty. Human stories have details that make them special and unique. Robot stories could belong to anyone.

Just because a robot sounds confident does not mean it's right. Your Job: Learn to check if facts are TRUE. Detective's Rule #1: If I cannot check it, I cannot trust it.” Archived from Educating AI (Nick Potkalitsky on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
